sweep_summary: Yidiny (yidi1250) is in the catalog as weight (CVV): stress on the first long vowel, else initial, alternating (Dixon 1977 grammar sec. 2.2, held only as Google Books snippets). Of the 13 title-hits (11 distinct works): three open full texts were downloaded and read — Hayes 1982 (brucehayes.org; image PDF, scanned), Nash 1979 (ANU open repository; image PDF, scanned) and Kager 1995 (Benjamins CC BY-NC) — plus Hagberg 1993/2006 (archive.org full view, text). All four confirm the catalog's classification; Hayes 1982 carries Dixon's rule verbatim as 'Stress Assignment (PRY 3)', i.e. Rule 3 of Dixon's 1977 LI article, and states the metrical version (disyllabic left-to-right feet, iambic only when a foot-final long vowel is present, else trochaic). Nash 1979 is the best new first-hand statement: it confirms the rule but reports from Dixon's and Hale's tapes that Stress Fronting to the initial syllable 'applies more often than not' in texts and that initial stress is perceptibly strongest — a caution that should be recorded next to Dixon's own sec. 2.6.1 and Babinski 2026 (JIPA, already held by the project), which codes Yidiny as fixed: initial syllable for its phonetic study. Crowhurst & Hewitt 1995 is paywalled; its abstract confirms alternation on even- vs odd-numbered syllables 'from Dixon 1977a: 40-41' (the catalog's locator). Bowern, Round & Alpher (in revision) remains unobtainable (no Crossref/lingbuzz/author-page copy; Round 2017 ROA-1313, downloaded, still cites it as 'in revision' and calls stress placement 'contentious') — highest acquisition priority. Not reachable: Nespor & Vogel 1986 (DOI paywalled), Halle & Vergnaud 1987 (print), Hung 1994 and Erwin 1994 (working-paper series, no online copies found). Flint 1970 is Aboriginal-English prosody, not relevant.

new_statements.reading: Nash (who attended Dixon's 1975 ANU lectures and listened to Dixon's and Hale's Yidiny tapes) confirms the underlying pattern the catalog codes — stress on the first long vowel (in odd-syllabled words the lengthened penult, so stress from syllable 2), otherwise on the initial syllable, alternating thereafter — but reports that in running text the phonetic Stress Fronting to the initial syllable 'applies more often than not', and (fn.3) that the initial stress in long-vowel-less words is perceptibly stronger than the others, which Dixon does not distinguish. Hayes 1982 (also downloaded, pp.99-100, 105) carries Dixon's rule verbatim and labels it Rule 3 of Dixon 1977a (the LI article), giving a full-text, paginated carry of the catalog's deciding quotation. Keep classification weight (CVV; first long vowel else initial, alternating); Nash's text-frequency observation belongs in the caution field alongside Dixon's sec. 2.6.1 and Babinski 2026 (which codes Yidiny as fixed: initial syllable for its phonetic study).

tone.quote: Figure 6 shows the effects found for stress on f0 range; most languages show no significant effect here, indicating that the shape of the tonal gesture does not change much in prominent syllables. In Bardi and Kayardild, f0 range is higher in stressed syllables, indicating a more extreme pitch excursion in prominent vowels. In Burarra and Yidiny, on the other hand, there are significant effects indicating a smaller f0 range in stressed syllables; this could indicate a steadier high tone on prominent syllables that varies less than in other contexts. However, any effects found here are relatively small, and it is not clear if strong conclusions can yet be drawn about the shape of pitch gestures.

sources.quote: When the underlying form has no long vowels, and an even number of syllables, all feet in the word are balanced trochees [LL] (8a-d). When a long vowel occurs in an even-numbered syllable, feet are iambic throughout the word (8e-f). Finally, when the word contains a special suffix that induces length in the preceding syllable, long vowels occur in odd-numbered syllables, with trochaic feet [LL] or [HL] (8g-h) ... We find that stress feet at word level are strictly disyllabic [LL], [LH], or [HL], excluding *[H]. Iambic [LL] occurs under pressure of prominence harmony only (Dixon 1977:41, McCarthy and Prince 1986).
sources.note: Sec. 2 'Yidiny' (pp.127-129) restates Dixon's system in foot terms: words with no long vowels and an even number of syllables have trochaic [LL] feet throughout; a long vowel in an even-numbered syllable makes all feet iambic; pre-suffixal length in odd-numbered syllables gives trochaic [LL]/[HL] feet; 'stress feet at word level are strictly disyllabic [LL], [LH], or [HL], excluding *[H]'. Data credited to Dixon 1977:41, 43. (The stressed example words in his (8) were lost in text extraction.) Consistent with the catalog's weight/long-vowel coding.

sources.citation: Hagberg, Lawrence Raymond. 1993. An autosegmental theory of stress. PhD dissertation, University of Arizona (UMI 9328564); reissued 2006 as SIL e-Book 3 (hdl 11858/00-001M-0000-0012-762C-9).
sources.quote: [p.205] Dixon's 1977 generalization regarding Yidiny stress is as follows (repeated from section 2.1.2.2): (1) Stress Assignment Rule (Dixon 1977): Stress is assigned to the first syllable involving a long vowel. If there is no long vowel, it is assigned to the first syllable of the word. Further stresses are then assigned (recursively) to the syllable next but one before, and the next but one after, a stressed syllable. ... Notice that long vowels are always stressed ... stress occurs either on every even-numbered syllable, as in (2), or on every odd-numbered syllable, as in (3), depending upon the location of long vowels. [p.206] If there are no long vowels, then stress occurs on odd-numbered syllables, as in (4).
sources.locator: pp. 62 (rule 14), 205-206 (rule 1 and data 2-4); djvu the text
sources.note: Sec. 2.1.2.2 (pp.61-63) and ch.4 'Headless feet in Yidiny' (pp.204-218) take all data from Dixon 1977, quote his Stress Assignment Rule verbatim as (14)/(1), and summarise: long vowels are always stressed; stress falls on every even-numbered syllable or every odd-numbered syllable depending on where long vowels are; with no long vowels, stress is on odd-numbered syllables (all such words even-syllabled). Analysis: syllabic feet built iteratively left to right, stress linked autosegmentally under the Weight-to-Stress Principle. Confirms the catalog's classification.

sources.quote: Metrical heads are later assigned to these constituents by independent rules operating under quantity-sensitive principles. In other words, Yidiny employs an additive metrical system in which stressable heads are overlaid on existing foot structures (prosodic overlay). It is the interaction between the outputs of these operations which produces the flexible rhythmic structure for which Yidiny is known. This flexibility is exemplified by the forms in (1a) and (1b) (from Dixon 1977a: 40–41), where stress falls on even-numbered and odd-numbered syllables respectively, counted from the left.
